titolo: Why Did Malaysia Get Rich But the Philippines Didn't?
descrizione:
Around 1960, the average Malaysian and the average Filipino earned about the same. Today the average Malaysian is more than three times as rich. Not the skylines. The paychecks. Same corner of Asia, same sea, both former colonies. So how did one neighbour pull three times ahead?

This is the economic history of Malaysia and the Philippines told on a 3D map: the Strait of Malacca and its ports, tin and rubber, Sabah and the old quarrel over it, FELDA's land for poor families, the riots of 1969 and the New Economic Policy, the Intel plant that opened in Penang in 1972, oil, Mahathir and the Petronas Towers, Marcos and the debt crash, the boom of the 1990s, Malaysia's capital controls in 1998, why the gap stopped growing around 2000, and where both countries stand today.

trascrizione_inizio: Around 1960, [music] the average Malaysian and the average Filipino earned about the same. Today, the average Malaysian is more than three times [music] as rich. Not the skylines, the paychecks. Same corner of Asia, same rain, same sea. Both were colonies and both became independent within 11 years of each other. >> [music] >> So, how did one neighbor pull three times ahead? Part of the answer is a single factory built in [music] 1972. But first, the map. Malaysia sits on the Strait of Malacca, the shortest sea route between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. [music] More than 100,000 ships pass through it every year. It is one of the busiest shipping lanes on Earth [music] and every ship that stops needs fuel, food, repairs, and someone to handle its cargo. >> [music] >> The British built ports along it. Penang became a free port in 1786. [music] Today, Port Klang, near Kuala Lumpur, is the 10th busiest container port in the world. The Philippines is more than 7,600 islands off to the side of that great sea route [music] and right in the path of about 20 tropical storms a year. Malaysia sits almost [music] entirely outside the typhoon belt. Under British rule, the Malay Peninsula dug up and grew what the industrial world wanted. [music] Around 1900, it produced more than half of the world's tin. Kuala Lumpur itself began as a tin miners camp where two muddy rivers meet. Then, came cars [music] and cars needed tires. By 1919, Malaya was exporting more rubber than the rest of the world combined. The mines were worked mostly by Chinese migrants. [music] The rubber estates, mostly by Indians. By 1931, about a third of the people in Malaya were Chinese and about one in seven was Indian. The Philippines, under American rule, mostly sold sugar to America. Malaya was selling to the whole world through one of its busiest seaways. The Philippines became independent in 1946. Malaya in 1957.
